conceptTag: Hotel towel signs and social proof
readerTitle: The hotel towel sign that worked better by saying less about the planet
caseNote: 실제 호텔 현장 실험 (Goldstein, Cialdini, Griskevicius 2008, 미국 애리조나의 중형 호텔, 호텔명 비공개) + 후속 재현 연구 + 가상 적용 (B2B 회계 서비스)
insight: 사람을 움직이는 건 '옳은 이유'보다 '나와 비슷한 사람들이 실제로 하는 일'이며, 그 무리가 가까울수록 힘이 세다.
misconception: 좋은 이유를 잘 설명하면 사람들이 따른다. 그리고 '많은 사람이 안 한다'고 경고하면 행동이 바뀐다.

sources.text: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., & Griskevicius, V. (2008). A Room with a Viewpoint: Using Social Norms to Motivate Environmental Conservation in Hotels. Journal of Consumer Research, 35(3), 472–482.
Bohner, G., & Schlüter, L. E. (2014). A Room with a Viewpoint Revisited: Descriptive Norms and Hotel Guests' Towel Reuse Behavior. PLOS ONE.
Scheibehenne, B., Jamil, T., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2016). Bayesian Evidence Synthesis Can Reconcile Seemingly Inconsistent Results: The Case of Hotel Towel Reuse. Psychological Science.
Cialdini, R. B. (2003). Crafting Normative Messages to Protect the Environment. Current Directions in Psychological Science (Petrified Forest 사례).
회계 서비스 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 연구 1의 수건 재사용률: 표준 환경 메시지 약 35.1%, '다른 투숙객 대부분이 재사용' 메시지 약 44.1%. 게시 전 원 논문(JCR 2008) 표와 다시 대조하세요.
연구 2의 '이 방에 묵었던 투숙객' 메시지가 가장 높았다(약 49%)는 점을 카드에 'nearly half'로만 적었습니다. 정확한 수치와 비교 조건을 원 논문에서 확인하세요.
호텔은 실제 호텔이지만 논문에서 이름이 공개되지 않았습니다. 카드에 호텔명을 쓰지 않았습니다. 지역(애리조나)은 확인 후에만 추가하세요.
독일 재현 연구(Bohner & Schlüter 2014)는 효과를 재현하지 못했고, 이후 종합 분석(Scheibehenne 외 2016)은 효과가 있되 작다고 결론. 카드에는 '작고 상황에 따라 다르다'로만 적었습니다.
Petrified Forest 국립공원 실험(나쁜 행동이 흔하다고 알리는 메시지가 역효과)은 Cialdini(2003)에 나옵니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The hotel towel sign that worked better by saying less about the planet
body: Hotels have long asked guests to reuse their towels. The usual sign talks about saving water and protecting nature.
In a real hotel, researchers tested a different sign. It didn't add a better reason. It added other people.

image.label: A small card hanging on a hotel bathroom towel rack
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 호텔 욕실. 수건걸이에 작은 안내 카드가 걸려 있고, 카드 문구는 흐릿하게 처리. 실제 호텔 로고나 브랜드 없음. 차분한 일러스트 스타일.

cards.title: Which card gets more towels reused?
body: You manage a mid-sized hotel. You can print one card for every bathroom. Guests see it once, alone, with no one watching.

options.text: "Help save the environment. Reuse your towels."
options.feedback: A sound reason, and some guests act on it. But it asks each guest to care about the planet on their own, which is a weak pull at 7 a.m.

options.text: "Most guests at this hotel reuse their towels. Join them."
options.feedback: This tells guests what normal looks like here. It gives up the moral argument and gains something stronger: a cue about what people like them do.

options.text: "Too many guests still don't reuse towels. Help us change that."
options.feedback: It sounds urgent, but it quietly tells guests that not reusing is common. You gain alarm and lose the norm.

cards.title: The crowd beat the cause.
body: In a 2008 study, researchers rotated cards across rooms. The only change was the message. Saying most guests reuse towels lifted reuse by about nine points.

groups.label: Guests who reused at least one towel

image.label: The crowd beat the cause.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Social proof: we copy people like us
body: **Social proof** is our habit of looking at what others do to decide what we should do. It is strongest when we are unsure and alone, like a guest in a hotel bathroom.
The environmental card told guests what was *right*. The winning card told them what was *normal*. Most people trust normal more than they admit.

cards.title: The closer the crowd, the stronger the pull.
body: In a second study, the team tried several versions of "other guests." The best one was oddly specific: guests who had stayed **in this same room**.
That card did best of all, with nearly half of guests reusing. A room number has nothing to do with towels. But it made the crowd feel close, like people in your exact situation.

image.label: Circles of people narrowing from 'guests' to 'this room'
image.brief: 동심원 인포그래픽. 바깥 원 "People", 가운데 "Guests at this hotel", 가장 안쪽 원 "Guests in this room". 안쪽으로 갈수록 색이 진해지고 화살표가 투숙객 아이콘을 가리킴.

cards.title: The same lever works on a store shelf.
body: A hardware chain could label a paint roller "bestseller." Better: "Most bought by customers at this store." A local crowd feels more like you than a national one.
The rule travels: show real behavior, from a group the customer sees as similar.
cards.softwareNote: In software, "Most teams your size turn on this setting" during onboarding often beats a list of benefits, as long as it's true for that segment of users.

cards.title: Social proof is real, but smaller and pickier than the headline.
body: A German team later tried to repeat the towel study and found no clear effect. A later analysis of the evidence concluded the effect exists but is small and depends on context.

It also needs to be true and needs a real majority. Research at a US national park suggests that signs saying many visitors steal wood can make theft seem normal. If most people don't do it yet, don't announce that.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You run a bookkeeping service for small businesses. Late receipts cause rushed, error-prone month-end work. Your records show 8 in 10 clients send documents by the 5th.
Which reminder email do you send?

options.text: "Late documents cause errors. Please send yours by the 5th."
options.feedback: Clear and honest. But it relies on a reason clients already know and ignore when they're busy.

options.text: "2 in 10 clients send documents late. Don't be one of them."
options.feedback: It feels pointed, but it puts the late group in the spotlight and makes lateness sound common.

options.text: "8 in 10 businesses like yours send their documents by the 5th."
options.feedback: It uses a true majority and a close crowd. You trade the lecture for a picture of what peers already do.

cards.title: Show people what others like them already do.
body: A good reason informs. A true, nearby norm moves. Pick the closest crowd you can honestly describe, and never advertise the bad behavior you want to stop.
**Try it today:** find one sign, email or form where you ask customers to do something. Rewrite it around what most similar customers already do, using a number you can prove.
